newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong stages grand gala bridge opening.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong stages grand gala bridge opening.

text.p: Hong Kong gave full rein to its party spirit on Sunday by celebrating the opening of its spectacular new suspension bridge in extravagent style barely a week after a suspected sabotage attempt.
Tens of thousands of people took part in the last big British bash before an exhaustive round of celebrations gets underway to mark the handover of the colony to China in just 65 days.
The world's longest road-rail suspension bridge is 2.14 km (1.33 miles) long and links Hong Kong to its new airport, taking shape off the island of Lantau and due to open in the middle of next year.
Fireworks and lasers lit up the night sky in a grand finale to a ceremony which began as a red sun slipped behind the undulating hills of the Kowloon peninsula.

As the shadows lengthened, former British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher, who signed the 1984 treaty governing the handover of Hong Kong to China, declared what she called "an impressive and inspiring entrance to this modern city" open.
"Standing here, at Hong Kong's gateway to the world, it (the bridge) is a visible sign of what Hong Kong represents, a rare and fruitful combination of diverse talents and cultures," Thatcher said.
For a moment the graceful span stood silhouetted against the darkening sky before a filigree of lights snapped along the full length of world's longest rail-road suspension bridge.
Curtains of fire dripped down from the bridge-deck -- a pyrotechnic special effect created specially for the occasion.

In the nearby bay bobbed a flotilla of boats. Floating gin palaces, Chinese junks and samans, cross-harbour ferries and even dredgers and tugs pressed into service by thousands of sightseers anchored under the watchful eyes of the Royal Naval Patrol vessel HMS Starling.
Anxiety about security ran high after cables at the bridge were cut by saboteurs or vandals earlier this month.
Police spokesman Colin Keenan said the authorities had drawn up security contingency plans to cover all eventualities -- including guerrilla attacks -- on or near the bridge.

Though pipped for the record of the world's longest suspension bridge -- Britain's Humber bridge holds that honour -- the Tsing Ma bridge holds the record as the longest road-rail bridge, satisfying Hong Kong's obsession with superlatives.
Hong Kong people love to boast of having the world's longest outdoor escalator, the world's busiest container port, and the greatest number of Rolls-Royce cars per head.
For Hong Kong, the HK$7.2-billion ($920-million) bridge, built by a Japanese-British joint venture and partially assembled in China, marks more than just an engineering feat.

The completion on schedule of a vital -- and very visible -- component in the US$20-billion airport project represents a practical victory over the political row that dogged Sino-ritish relations on Hong Kong during the countdown.
China denounced the project as extravagent and accused the British of trying to squander Hong Kong's wealth.
The bickering dragged on for more than five years before agreement was finally reached in 1995. But in the meantime, the Hong Kong government quietly got on with the work.
